en.title: Optometry: the whole course
en.short: What optometry is, how the degree is organised, the main areas and how to study it.

sections.heading: Read this first
sections.text: These notes teach optometry concepts to students. They are not medical advice and do not replace supervision, textbooks or official guidance. They do not give drug doses. Clinical guidelines change and differ between countries, so check the current national guidance or World Health Organization (WHO) source before applying anything. Anyone with eye pain, sudden vision loss, injury or another urgent problem should seek local clinical help at once. Scope of practice is set by law and by the regulator in each country, so do not assume that a task allowed in one place is allowed in another.

sections.heading: What optometry is
sections.text: Optometry is the health profession concerned with the eye and the visual system. It covers refraction, the measurement of refractive error and the prescription of spectacles or contact lenses; dispensing and ophthalmic optics; binocular vision; the detection and management of some eye disease; low vision; and public eye health. Optometrists work in clinics, hospitals, practices, industry and community programmes. Their exact scope varies by country. In many places they diagnose and manage refractive error, prescribe optical correction, fit contact lenses and monitor eye health, and refer surgical or complex medical cases to an ophthalmologist, a medically qualified eye doctor. Optometry is not ophthalmology, though the two work together.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text: Degrees have several names, including Doctor of Optometry (OD), BSc Optometry and BOptom. Length and award differ by country and institution. In Nigeria, optometry is usually a six-year university programme leading to the OD degree, with registration through the Optometrists and Dispensing Opticians Registration Board of Nigeria; internship and registration rules are set by the board, so check its current requirements. In the United Kingdom, the usual route is a three-year BSc Optometry followed by a pre-registration period for registration with the General Optical Council. In the United States, the OD is a four-year professional degree taken after undergraduate study. These are common patterns, not universal rules. Always check your own faculty handbook and regulator.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Teaching usually moves from foundations to clinical core and then to advanced study. The introductory stage covers the profession and scope; ocular anatomy and physiology; head, neck and neuroanatomy; geometrical optics; physical optics and photometry; visual optics and accommodation; mathematics and statistics; and ocular microbiology with infection control. These subjects explain how light forms an image, how the eye and visual pathway work, and how infection is prevented.

The core stage applies that knowledge. It includes refractive error and refraction; ophthalmic optics and spectacle dispensing; binocular vision and strabismus; contact lens practice; ocular pharmacology; anterior segment and adnexal disease; posterior segment disease; glaucoma; systemic disease and the eye; paediatric optometry; low vision and rehabilitation; ocular emergencies and trauma; public health optometry; ethics, law and professionalism; and clinical case management.

At master’s level, common topics are advanced ocular imaging and diagnostics, advanced contact lens practice and the ocular surface, advanced binocular vision and vision therapy, and research methods with a dissertation. Exact modules vary by school.

sections.heading: How to study optometry
sections.text: Start with normal structure and function, then link each disorder to the mechanism it disturbs. In optics, draw ray diagrams and do the calculations by hand until they are reliable. In anatomy, draw and label from memory. In refraction, practise on fellow students under supervision and record what you did. Use spaced self-testing rather than rereading alone. Work through case questions: what is the complaint, what tests are needed, what is the likely diagnosis, and when should you refer? Learn the local laws and referral pathways. Keep a log of clinical skills and ask a tutor to check your technique.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Students often memorise lists without mechanisms, so they cannot reason through a new case. Some confuse optometry with ophthalmology or forget that scope of practice is set by national law. Others ignore the mathematics and optics that explain instruments and lenses. In clinics, a common error is to jump to a diagnosis before taking a careful history and checking visual acuity, pupils and the front and back of the eye. Another is to quote one country’s guideline as universal. Never diagnose or treat yourself or friends from notes such as these; seek a qualified clinician.

keyPoints: Optometry is a health profession covering refraction, optical correction, binocular vision, eye health and low vision, with a scope set by national law.
Degree length and award vary: Nigeria commonly uses a six-year OD, the UK a BSc plus pre-registration, and the US a four-year OD after undergraduate study.
Study normal anatomy, physiology and optics first, then apply them to refractive error, disease and clinical case management.
Practise practical skills and calculations under supervision, and test yourself with spaced questions and cases.
Clinical guidelines change and differ between countries, so check current national or WHO guidance.
These notes teach concepts and are not medical advice; they do not give drug doses.

en.title: Optometry as a profession: history, roles and scope
en.short: History, roles, scope, regulation and referral in optometry as a health profession.

sections.heading: Origins and identity
sections.text: Optometry is the health profession concerned with the eye and vision, especially refraction, the measurement of the eye’s focusing error, and eye health screening. It grew from spectacle making and lens grinding. In many countries it became a regulated profession, but the timing and training route differ. Some optometrists begin with a diploma and later upgrade; others complete a university degree. The profession’s identity rests on measuring vision, correcting refractive error and recognising eye disease.

sections.heading: Roles and scope
sections.text: Roles include primary eye care, refraction, fitting spectacles or contact lenses where allowed, low vision support and screening for disease. Scope of practice is the set of tasks a profession is legally and ethically permitted to do. It varies by country. Some optometrists may use diagnostic drugs or prescribe medicines; others may not. Check the national regulator’s current rules. Case: Amina, a teacher in Kano, has blurred vision. A community health worker refers her to an optometrist, who checks vision and refers onward for sudden loss, pain or other warning signs.

sections.heading: Regulation and organisations
sections.text: Regulation protects the public. A regulator registers qualified practitioners, sets entry standards, approves courses and handles complaints. Professional associations, such as the Nigerian Optometric Association, promote education and advocacy but do not replace the regulator. In Nigeria the Optometrists and Dispensing Opticians Registration Board of Nigeria is the legal regulator. Names and powers differ elsewhere. The World Council of Optometry is an international professional body. Continuing professional development, meaning ongoing learning after qualification, is usually required.

sections.heading: Teamwork and referral
sections.text: Eye care is interprofessional: optometrists, ophthalmologists, dispensing opticians (who fit and supply spectacles), nurses, pharmacists and community workers each contribute. An ophthalmologist is a medical doctor who treats eye disease and performs surgery. A referral pathway is the agreed route by which a patient moves from one level of care to another. Clear pathways prevent delay. Urgent warning signs need same-day referral under local guidance. Clinical guidelines change and differ between countries, so use current national or World Health Organization guidance.

keyPoints: Optometry grew from spectacle making and refraction and became a regulated profession at different times in different countries.
Scope of practice is the set of tasks the law and professional standards allow, and it varies by country.
Regulators register practitioners and protect the public; professional associations support education and advocacy.
In Nigeria, the Optometrists and Dispensing Opticians Registration Board of Nigeria is the legal regulator.
Optometrists work with ophthalmologists, nurses, pharmacists and community workers in interprofessional eye care.
A referral pathway is the agreed route for moving a patient to the right level of care, and urgent warning signs need prompt referral under local guidance.

en.title: Ocular anatomy: the eye and its adnexa
en.short: The gross and microscopic structure of the eye, its coats, contents, lids, lacrimal system, orbit and muscles.

sections.heading: The globe
sections.text: The globe is the eyeball. It has three coats. The outer fibrous coat is the clear cornea in front and the white sclera behind. The middle vascular coat is the uvea: iris, ciliary body and choroid. The inner neural coat is the retina. The cornea has five main layers: epithelium, Bowman’s layer, stroma, Descemet’s membrane and endothelium. It is avascular and richly supplied by nerves from the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve. The sclera is dense collagen. The uvea supplies blood and pigment; the iris controls the pupil, and the ciliary body holds the lens by zonules.

sections.heading: Inside the eye
sections.text: The lens is a transparent biconvex structure with a capsule, epithelium, cortex and nucleus. The vitreous is a clear gel filling the space behind the lens. The retina lines the back of the eye. Microscopically it has a pigment epithelium and neural layers. Signals pass from photoreceptors to bipolar cells to ganglion cells, whose axons form the optic nerve. The optic nerve is cranial nerve II; it carries visual signals and is wrapped in meninges. The macula and fovea are central retinal areas for sharp vision.

sections.heading: Adnexa and orbit
sections.text: The adnexa are the structures around the globe. The lids protect the eye. Each lid has skin, orbicularis oculi muscle, tarsal plate, conjunctiva and glands, including meibomian glands. The lacrimal system includes the lacrimal gland, puncta, canaliculi, lacrimal sac and nasolacrimal duct. Tears drain into the nose. The orbit is the bony cavity that holds the eye, fat, vessels and nerves. Six extraocular muscles move each eye: four recti and two obliques. The levator palpebrae superioris raises the upper lid.

sections.heading: Case example
sections.text: A student, Ada, asks why a small corneal scratch is painful and makes the eye water. The cornea has many sensory nerve endings, so injury triggers pain and reflex tearing. The tear film and lid blinking protect the surface. This links microscopic anatomy to symptoms: corneal nerves, lid glands and lacrimal drainage all work together.

keyPoints: The globe has three coats: cornea and sclera, uvea, and retina.
The cornea has five layers and is avascular but richly innervated.
The uvea is the iris, ciliary body and choroid.
The retina’s ganglion cell axons form the optic nerve.
The adnexa include lids, lacrimal system, orbit and extraocular muscles.
Four recti and two obliques move the eye; the levator raises the upper lid.

en.title: Ocular physiology: ocular fluids, transparency and light signalling
en.short: Tear film, cornea, aqueous, lens, vitreous, phototransduction, retinal processing and pupil reflexes.

sections.heading: Tear film and cornea
sections.text:
The tear film is a thin coating over the ocular surface. It has a mucus layer next to the epithelium, an aqueous layer carrying water, salts and proteins, and a lipid layer from the meibomian glands that slows evaporation. Tears lubricate, protect and smooth the surface.

The cornea is clear because its collagen fibres form a regular lattice and the endothelium keeps it dehydrated. In wound healing, epithelial cells migrate and divide, stromal cells make new matrix, and the endothelium does not regenerate. Scarring can reduce transparency.

sections.heading: Aqueous, lens and vitreous
sections.text:
Aqueous humour is fluid in the anterior and posterior chambers. The ciliary epithelium secretes it. It leaves mainly through the trabecular meshwork and Schlemm canal, and some by the uveoscleral route. Intraocular pressure depends on the balance between formation and outflow. For example, if formation is 2.5 microlitres per minute and outflow facility is 0.25 microlitres per minute per mmHg, formation divided by facility is 10 mmHg; adding episcleral venous pressure of 10 mmHg gives 20 mmHg. These are illustrative only.

The lens is avascular and transparent. It relies on anaerobic glycolysis and ordered crystallin proteins. The vitreous is a gel of collagen and hyaluronan that supports the retina and transmits light.

sections.heading: Phototransduction and retina
sections.text:
Phototransduction converts light into a nerve signal. In rods, light changes rhodopsin, which activates transducin, then phosphodiesterase. This lowers cyclic GMP, closes sodium channels and hyperpolarises the cell. Cones work similarly but serve colour and detail.

The retina processes signals. Bipolar cells pass signals to ganglion cells. Horizontal and amacrine cells create centre-surround receptive fields, which sharpen contrast. Ganglion cell axons form the optic nerve.

sections.heading: Pupil reflexes
sections.text: The pupil reflex needs an intact optic nerve and oculomotor pathway. Light in one eye signals the pretectal area, then both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, so both pupils constrict: direct and consensual reflexes. The near response adds accommodation and convergence. A relative afferent pupillary defect suggests optic nerve disease. Clinical tests vary, so follow current local guidance.

keyPoints: The tear film has mucus, aqueous and lipid layers; tears lubricate, protect and smooth the surface.
Corneal transparency depends on regular collagen and relative dehydration; endothelial cells usually do not regenerate.
Aqueous humour is secreted by the ciliary epithelium and drains through the trabecular meshwork and Schlemm canal.
The Goldmann relation is IOP = F/C + Pv, where F is aqueous formation, C is outflow facility and Pv is episcleral venous pressure.
The lens is avascular and uses mainly anaerobic glycolysis; the vitreous is a collagen and hyaluronan gel.
Phototransduction in rods lowers cyclic GMP, closes sodium channels and hyperpolarises the cell; retinal centre-surround fields sharpen contrast.

en.title: Head, neck and neuroanatomy for optometry
en.short: Skull and orbit bones, cranial nerves, eye muscles, visual and pupillary pathways.

sections.heading: Skull and orbit
sections.text: The skull has cranial bones (frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid) and facial bones (zygomatic, maxilla, nasal, lacrimal, palatine, vomer, inferior concha, mandible). The orbit is a bony pyramid that protects the eye. Its walls are formed by seven bones: frontal, zygomatic, maxilla, sphenoid, ethmoid, lacrimal and palatine. The optic canal carries the optic nerve; the superior orbital fissure carries cranial nerves III, IV, V1 and VI. This is anatomy teaching, not clinical advice.

sections.heading: Cranial nerves and muscles
sections.text: Twelve pairs of cranial nerves arise from the brain. For optometry, II optic, III oculomotor, IV trochlear, V trigeminal (V1 ophthalmic), VI abducens and VII facial. Extraocular muscles are four recti and two obliques. Medial rectus adducts; lateral rectus abducts. Superior rectus elevates, adducts and intorts; inferior rectus depresses, adducts and extorts. Superior oblique depresses, abducts and intorts; inferior oblique elevates, abducts and extorts. Actions depend on gaze. Lateral rectus is VI, superior oblique IV, the rest III. Levator palpebrae superioris is III.

sections.heading: Visual pathway
sections.text: Light falls on the retina, where photoreceptors convert it to nerve signals. These travel in the optic nerve. At the optic chiasm, nasal retinal fibres cross; temporal fibres stay on the same side. The optic tract carries signals to the lateral geniculate nucleus, a thalamic relay. Optic radiations reach the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe. A lesion before the chiasm affects one eye; after it, part of both visual fields.

sections.heading: Pupil and autonomic
sections.text: The efferent limb of the pupillary light reflex is parasympathetic. Light in one eye travels via the optic nerve and tract to the pretectal nucleus, then to both Edinger-Westphal nuclei. Fibres run with III to the ciliary ganglion, then short ciliary nerves to the sphincter pupillae, constricting both pupils. Accommodation shares this parasympathetic route: the ciliary muscle contracts and the lens rounds. Convergence of the eyes is a separate part of the near response, driven by III to the medial recti. Sympathetic fibres from the superior cervical ganglion dilate the pupil and help lift the lid. A fixed dilated pupil with ptosis after head injury suggests III palsy and needs urgent assessment.

keyPoints: The orbit is formed by seven bones: frontal, zygomatic, maxilla, sphenoid, ethmoid, lacrimal and palatine.
Cranial nerves II to VII relevant to the eye are optic, oculomotor, trochlear, trigeminal (V1), abducens and facial.
Lateral rectus is supplied by VI, superior oblique by IV, and other extraocular muscles by III.
The visual pathway runs retina, optic nerve, chiasm, optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus, optic radiation, occipital cortex.
Parasympathetic fibres constrict the pupil and drive accommodation; sympathetic fibres dilate the pupil.
A fixed dilated pupil with ptosis after head injury suggests III palsy and needs urgent assessment.

en.title: Geometrical optics
en.short: Rays, reflection, refraction, prisms, lenses, mirrors, cardinal points, instruments and ray tracing.

sections.heading: Light and reflection
sections.text: Geometrical optics treats light as rays that travel in straight lines in a uniform medium, called rectilinear propagation. This explains shadows and pinhole images. At a surface, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal. A plane mirror forms a virtual image behind it, same size and laterally inverted. A concave mirror converges light; a convex mirror diverges it.

sections.heading: Refraction and prisms
sections.text: Refraction is bending when light crosses a boundary between media of different refractive index n, where n = c/v and c is the speed of light in vacuum. Snell’s law: n1 sin θ1 = n2 sin θ2, angles from the normal. Light bends towards the normal entering a denser medium. A prism has two non-parallel surfaces and deviates light towards its base. Total internal reflection occurs above the critical angle C, where sin C = n2/n1 for n1 > n2. Prisms in spectacles displace images.

sections.heading: Lenses and cardinal points
sections.text: A lens refracts at two surfaces. A thin lens has negligible thickness; a thick lens has significant thickness and is described by cardinal points: two focal points, two principal points and two nodal points. For a thin lens, 1/f = 1/u + 1/v, where f is focal length, u object distance and v image distance, positive for real distances. Example: f = 10 cm, u = 30 cm, so 1/v = 1/10 − 1/30 = 1/15, v = 15 cm. The image is real and inverted; magnification magnitude is v/u = 0.5. Sign conventions vary; use one consistently.

sections.heading: Mirrors instruments ray tracing
sections.text: Spherical mirrors obey 1/f = 1/u + 1/v, with f = R/2 for radius R, using a consistent sign convention. Ray tracing uses simple rays: a ray parallel to the axis passes through the focal point after a converging lens or concave mirror; a ray through the optical centre continues straight; a ray through the focal point emerges parallel. Telescopes, microscopes and cameras combine lenses or mirrors to form images.

keyPoints: Light travels in straight lines in a uniform medium, and the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
Refraction follows Snell’s law, n1 sin θ1 = n2 sin θ2, where n = c/v.
A prism deviates light towards its base; total internal reflection begins at the critical angle C, where sin C = n2/n1 for n1 > n2.
For a thin lens, 1/f = 1/u + 1/v, and the magnification magnitude is v/u; sign conventions vary, so use one consistently.
A thick lens is described by cardinal points: two focal, two principal and two nodal points.
Spherical mirrors obey 1/f = 1/u + 1/v with f = R/2, and ray tracing uses rays parallel to the axis, through the optical centre and through the focal point.

en.title: Physical optics and photometry
en.short: Wave optics, polarisation, scattering, photometry units and laser safety for first-year optometry.

sections.heading: Wave nature and interference
sections.text: Light is an electromagnetic wave with speed c, where c = fλ (f frequency, λ wavelength). Visible light is roughly 380 to 750 nm. Interference is superposition of waves. Constructive interference gives a bright fringe when path difference is mλ; destructive gives a dark fringe at (m + ½)λ. Young’s double slit shows this. Diffraction is spreading at an edge or aperture. A single slit gives minima where a sinθ = mλ. Diffraction limits the resolution of optical instruments.

sections.heading: Polarisation and scattering
sections.text: Polarisation is the direction of the electric field oscillation. Light is transverse, so it can be polarised. A polariser transmits one plane of oscillation. Reflected glare from water or car paint is partly polarised, so polarising sunglasses reduce it. Scattering redirects light. Rayleigh scattering, from particles much smaller than the wavelength, varies as 1/λ⁴; it makes the sky blue. Mie scattering, from larger particles, is less wavelength-dependent. In the eye, scattering causes glare and reduces contrast, as in cataract.

sections.heading: Photometry and units
sections.text: Photometry measures light as the human eye sees it, weighted by the luminous efficiency function V(λ), which peaks near 555 nm. The lumen (lm) is luminous flux. The candela (cd) is luminous intensity. Illuminance, in lux (lx), is flux per square metre (lm/m²). Luminance, in cd/m², is light leaving a surface. For a point source, E = I/d². Example: a 100 cd lamp at 2 m gives E = 100 ÷ 2² = 100 ÷ 4 = 25 lx. Doubling distance quarters illuminance.

sections.heading: Sources and laser safety
sections.text: Light sources include thermal emitters (incandescent), discharge lamps (fluorescent), solid-state emitters (LEDs) and lasers. Lasers produce coherent, monochromatic, collimated light, so even low power can damage the retina. Laser safety: know the class, never look into the beam or its specular reflection, use eyewear matched to the wavelength, control the area, use signs, and follow the local laser safety officer and current national or IEC standards. This is not medical advice.

keyPoints: Light is an electromagnetic wave; c = fλ, and visible light is roughly 380 to 750 nm.
Interference is constructive at path difference mλ and destructive at (m + ½)λ; single-slit diffraction minima occur at a sinθ = mλ.
Polarisation is the plane of electric field oscillation; polarising lenses reduce reflected glare.
Rayleigh scattering varies as 1/λ⁴ and explains the blue sky; scattering in the eye causes glare.
Photometry units: lumen (flux), candela (intensity), lux (illuminance), cd/m² (luminance); E = I/d² for a point source.
Lasers are coherent, monochromatic and collimated; follow laser class rules, use matched eyewear and local safety standards.

en.title: Visual optics and accommodation
en.short: The eye as an optical system, schematic eyes, retinal image size, accommodation and refractive error.

sections.heading: The eye as an optical system
sections.text: The eye is a refracting system that forms a real, inverted image on the retina. The cornea supplies most fixed power, about 43 D, and the crystalline lens adds variable power, about 19 D, giving a total near 60 D in a typical adult. A dioptre (D) is 1/metre and measures power. Light from a distant object arrives almost parallel and is focused by the cornea and lens. The iris controls pupil size, which affects light entering and blur.

sections.heading: Schematic eyes and cardinal points
sections.text: A schematic eye is a simplified model of the eye’s optics. The reduced eye uses one refracting surface and a single power. The Gullstrand exact eye uses several surfaces. Cardinal points describe an optical system: two focal points, two principal points and two nodal points. The principal points lie close together just behind the cornea; the nodal points lie near the posterior lens. A ray through a nodal point passes undeviated, so retinal image size follows from the nodal point.

sections.heading: Retinal image size and accommodation
sections.text: For a distant object, retinal image size h' = θ × 16.7 mm, where θ is the angular size in radians. Example: a 1.5 m tall person at 20 m subtends θ = 1.5 ÷ 20 = 0.075 rad, so h' = 0.075 × 16.7 = 1.25 mm. Accommodation is the increase in lens power for near vision. The ciliary muscle contracts, the zonules (the fibres that hold the lens in place) relax and the lens becomes more convex. Amplitude of accommodation is the maximum increase in power, in dioptres.

sections.heading: Depth of focus, refractive error and acuity
sections.text: Depth of focus is the range of retinal image positions that still gives acceptable blur; a smaller pupil increases it. Myopia focuses distant light in front of the retina, hyperopia behind it, and astigmatism gives different power in different meridians. Visual acuity is the ability to resolve detail. It depends on focus, pupil size, cone spacing and neural processing. Charts and pass standards vary by country, so check current local guidance.

keyPoints: The eye forms a real inverted retinal image; the cornea gives most fixed power and the lens variable power.
A dioptre is 1/metre; total power is about 60 D in a typical adult eye.
Cardinal points are two focal, two principal and two nodal points; rays through nodal points pass undeviated.
Retinal image size for a distant object: h' = θ × 16.7 mm, with θ in radians.
Accommodation raises lens power; ciliary contraction relaxes zonules and makes the lens more convex.
Myopia focuses in front of the retina, hyperopia behind it, astigmatism varies by meridian; acuity also depends on pupil, cones and neural processing.

en.title: Mathematics and statistics for optometry
en.short: Algebra, trigonometry, calculus, measurement, statistics, probability, hypothesis tests and data presentation.

sections.heading: Algebra and graphs
sections.text:
Algebra uses letters for unknown or changing quantities. A variable can change; a constant is fixed. Solve a linear equation by doing the same operation to both sides: if 2x + 3 = 11, then x = 4.

A function pairs each input with one output. A graph plots one variable against another. The slope of a straight line is change in y divided by change in x. Read axes, units and scale before interpreting a graph.

sections.heading: Trigonometry and calculus
sections.text:
Trigonometry deals with angles and triangles. In a right triangle, sine = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cosine = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, and tangent = opposite ÷ adjacent. Angles may be in degrees or radians; 180 degrees = π radians.

Calculus studies change and accumulation. A derivative gives a rate of change; an integral gives area under a curve. These tools help describe growth, decay and cumulative effects.

sections.heading: Measurement and errors
sections.text:
Measurement compares a quantity with a standard unit. Accuracy means closeness to the true value; precision means closeness of repeated values to each other. Random error scatters results; systematic error shifts them all in one direction.

Report units and sensible significant figures. Do not write more digits than the instrument supports. Calibration and repeated readings reduce error, but no measurement is perfect.

sections.heading: Statistics and testing
sections.text:
Descriptive statistics summarise data. Mean = Σx ÷ n; median is the middle value; mode is most frequent. Standard deviation measures spread: s = √(Σ(x − xbar)² ÷ (n − 1)). Example: 2, 4, 4, 6. Mean = 16 ÷ 4 = 4. Squared deviations sum to 8; variance = 8 ÷ 3 = 2.67; s = √2.67 = 1.63.

Probability measures chance from 0 to 1; for independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). Hypothesis testing compares a null hypothesis with data. A p-value is not the probability that the null is true. Present data in clear tables and labelled graphs with honest axes.

keyPoints: Solve equations by applying the same operation to both sides; check by substitution.
Sine = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cosine = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, tangent = opposite ÷ adjacent; 180 degrees = π radians.
A derivative is a rate of change; an integral is area under a curve.
Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated values; report units and sensible significant figures.
Mean = Σx ÷ n; sample standard deviation s = √(Σ(x − xbar)² ÷ (n − 1)).
For independent events P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B); a p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

en.title: Ocular microbiology and infection control
en.short: Normal eye flora, common ocular pathogens, transmission, hand hygiene, sterilisation and outbreak basics.

sections.heading: Normal flora and pathogens
sections.text: The healthy conjunctiva and lids carry normal flora, mainly coagulase-negative staphylococci, diphtheroids (Corynebacterium species) and Cutibacterium acnes (formerly Propionibacterium acnes). These usually cause no harm, but can infect when defences break down. Common pathogens include Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Pseudomonas is linked to contact lens keratitis. Adenovirus causes epidemic keratoconjunctivitis. Chlamydia trachomatis causes trachoma and inclusion conjunctivitis. Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes severe neonatal conjunctivitis. Acanthamoeba and Fusarium are contact lens related.

sections.heading: Transmission and hand hygiene
sections.text: Infection spreads by direct contact with fingers, eye secretions, contaminated lenses, cases, solutions, towels, tonometer prisms and other instruments. Droplets spread adenovirus. Standard precautions apply to every patient. Hand hygiene is the most effective single measure. Clean hands before and after patient contact, after touching equipment and after body fluids. Use soap and water when hands are visibly dirty; otherwise an alcohol-based rub is suitable. Do not touch your own face or clean equipment with contaminated gloves.

sections.heading: Sterilisation and disinfection
sections.text: Sterilisation kills all microorganisms, including bacterial spores; autoclaving is the usual method for reusable instruments. Disinfection reduces pathogens but may not kill spores. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions for chemical disinfection of tonometer prisms and trial lenses. Contact lens hygiene: wash and dry hands, rub and rinse lenses with fresh multipurpose solution, never use tap water, replace cases regularly, and do not sleep in lenses unless prescribed.

sections.heading: Outbreaks and a case
sections.text: An outbreak is more cases than expected in a place and time. Principles: recognise and report, isolate or cohort cases, strengthen hand hygiene, clean equipment, and notify public health authorities. Case: Amina, a student, presents with a painful red eye after swimming and sleeping in her lenses. Pseudomonas keratitis is suspected. She is referred urgently; her lens case and solution are discarded. National infection control guidance and WHO guidance should be checked because details differ by country.

keyPoints: Normal ocular flora includes coagulase-negative staphylococci and diphtheroids, which can become opportunistic.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a major cause of contact lens related keratitis.
Hand hygiene is the most effective single measure to prevent transmission.
Sterilisation kills all microorganisms including spores, while disinfection may not.
Contact lens hygiene means clean hands, fresh solution, no tap water and regular case replacement.
Report suspected outbreaks and follow current national or WHO infection control guidance.

en.title: Refractive error and refraction
en.short: Refraction: myopia, hyperopia, astigmatism, presbyopia; retinoscopy, prescribing and referral.

sections.heading: Refractive errors
sections.text: Refractive error means the eye’s optics do not focus parallel light on the retina when accommodation is relaxed. In myopia the image forms in front of the retina, usually because the eye is too long or the cornea too curved; distance vision is blurred and a minus (concave) lens corrects it. In hyperopia the image would form behind the retina; a plus (convex) lens corrects it, and young people may accommodate. Astigmatism has different power in different meridians, so a point becomes a line; a cylindrical lens corrects it. Presbyopia is age-related loss of accommodation from lens stiffening, corrected with a near addition.

sections.heading: Objective refraction
sections.text: Objective refraction measures the eye without asking the patient to choose lenses. Retinoscopy shines light into the eye and observes the red reflex. The examiner moves the streak and adds lenses until the reflex neutralises. The gross result includes the working distance, so subtract its power: net = gross − 1/d, with d in metres. For example, at 50 cm the working distance power is 1/0.50 = +2.00 D. A gross finding of +3.00 DS gives +3.00 − 2.00 = +1.00 DS. Autorefractors also give objective estimates, but they need checking.

sections.heading: Subjective refraction and prescribing
sections.text: Subjective refraction asks the patient which lens is clearer. It refines sphere, then cylinder and axis, often with a Jackson cross cylinder, and checks binocular balance. Prescribe only what helps symptoms and visual needs. Consider age, occupation, driving, reading, anisometropia and tolerance. Spectacle power, lens type and fitting belong to dispensing, but the refraction must be accurate. Guidelines for children, drivers and occupational safety vary by country; check current national guidance.

sections.heading: Referral
sections.text: Refer when vision does not improve with refraction, or when findings suggest disease: sudden loss, pain, redness, flashes, floaters, trauma, or a child with poor vision or unequal refractive error. High or unequal errors and suspected keratoconus need assessment. Referral pathways and legal scope differ by country, so follow local and current national or World Health Organization guidance.

keyPoints: Refractive error is a mismatch between the eye’s optical power and its axial length.
Myopia is corrected with a minus lens, hyperopia with a plus lens, astigmatism with a cylinder and presbyopia with a near addition.
Net retinoscopy = gross finding − working distance power, where working distance power = 1/d in metres.
Objective refraction includes retinoscopy and autorefraction; subjective refraction refines the result with patient responses.
Prescribe for symptoms and visual needs, not the number alone.
Refer sudden vision loss, pain, trauma, flashes, floaters, or vision that does not improve with refraction.

en.title: Ophthalmic optics and spectacle dispensing
en.short: Lens power and form, thickness, prisms, aberrations, materials, coatings, frames, centration, fitting and standards.

sections.heading: Lens power and form
sections.text: Lens power F is measured in dioptres (D): F = 1/f, with f in metres. Surface power depends on curvature and refractive index: F = (n − 1)/r, with r in metres and signs by convention. A thin lens combines surfaces: F = F1 + F2. Form means the chosen front and back curves. A meniscus lens has one convex and one concave surface; base curve is the front curve. For a +6.00 D lens, if the front curve is +9.00 D, the back curve is −3.00 D (6 = 9 + (−3)).

sections.heading: Thickness, prisms and aberrations
sections.text: Thickness is set by power, lens size and refractive index. Plus lenses are thickest at the centre; minus lenses at the edge. A prism deviates light toward its base and is measured in prism dioptres (Δ). Prentice’s rule gives induced prism: P = c × F, where c is decentration in centimetres. A +6.00 D lens decentred 4 mm (0.4 cm) induces 0.4 × 6 = 2.4 Δ. Aberrations include spherical aberration, coma, oblique astigmatism, distortion and chromatic aberration. Aspheric or well-chosen base curves reduce them.

sections.heading: Materials, coatings and frames
sections.text: Materials include hard resin (CR-39), polycarbonate, high-index plastics and glass. Polycarbonate is impact resistant but has a lower Abbe number, so more chromatic aberration. The Abbe number measures dispersion. Coatings include hard scratch-resistant, anti-reflection, hydrophobic, oleophobic and UV-blocking layers. Photochromic lenses darken in ultraviolet light. Frame choice considers face shape, bridge and temple fit, lens size, weight and intended use. A frame that is too large increases lens thickness and weight.

sections.heading: Centration, fitting and standards
sections.text: Centration aligns the optical centre, or the fitting cross of a progressive (varifocal) lens, with the pupil. Measure monocular pupillary distances and fitting height. Fitting checks vertex distance (lens-to-eye gap), pantoscopic tilt (frame front angle) and frame stability. Standards include ISO and national standards for lens power tolerances, transmittance and frame dimensions; requirements differ by country; check current standards. Dispensing records should include lens type, power, centration and frame measurements.

keyPoints: Lens power in dioptres is F = 1/f, with f in metres.
Surface power is F = (n − 1)/r; thin lens power is the sum of surface powers.
Plus lenses are centre-thick and minus lenses are edge-thick.
Prentice’s rule: P = c × F, with c in centimetres, gives induced prism in prism dioptres.
Aberrations include spherical aberration, coma, oblique astigmatism, distortion and chromatic aberration.
Centration and fitting check pupillary distance, fitting height, vertex distance and pantoscopic tilt against current standards.

en.title: Binocular vision and strabismus
en.short: Vergence, binocular single vision, suppression, amblyopia, heterophoria, strabismus and basic care.

sections.heading: Vergence and accommodation
sections.text: Vergence is coordinated movement of the two eyes to keep images on corresponding retinal points. Convergence turns the eyes inward for near targets; divergence turns them outward for distant targets. Accommodation is the increase in lens power to focus near objects. Near fixation usually drives both. Accommodation demand in dioptres is 1 divided by target distance in metres. Total convergence demand for a midline target is approximately 10 × interpupillary distance in millimetres divided by distance in centimetres. Example: 60 mm interpupillary distance at 40 cm gives 10 × 60 ÷ 40 = 15 prism dioptres; accommodation demand is 1 ÷ 0.40 = 2.50 D.

sections.heading: Single vision and suppression
sections.text: Binocular single vision is fusion of the two retinal images into one stable percept. It needs clear, similar images, normal alignment and intact visual pathways. Corresponding retinal points give the same visual direction. Suppression is cortical inhibition of one eye’s image, usually to avoid diplopia; it may become habitual. Amblyopia is reduced best-corrected visual acuity in one or both eyes from abnormal visual experience during the critical period, without visible structural cause. Main types are strabismic, refractive and deprivation amblyopia.

sections.heading: Heterophoria and strabismus
sections.text: Heterophoria is a latent deviation that fusion keeps controlled; it becomes manifest when fusion is broken. Heterotropia is a manifest deviation. Strabismus is any manifest misalignment: esotropia (inward), exotropia (outward), hypertropia (upward) or hypotropia (downward). It may be comitant, similar in all gaze directions, or incomitant, varying with gaze and often caused by paresis.

sections.heading: Assessment and management
sections.text: Assessment includes visual acuity, cover and alternate cover tests, prism cover test, Hirschberg and Krimsky tests, Worth 4-dot and Bagolini tests, stereoacuity, near point of convergence, accommodation amplitude and cycloplegic refraction. Management starts with correcting refractive error and treating amblyopia, using occlusion or atropine only under current guidelines. Vision therapy may help convergence insufficiency; prisms or surgery may help selected strabismus. Check current national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Vergence keeps images on corresponding retinal points; accommodation focuses near objects, and the two are linked.
Accommodation demand (D) = 1 ÷ distance in metres; total convergence demand ≈ 10 × PD(mm) ÷ distance(cm).
Binocular single vision needs alignment, similar images and intact pathways; suppression is cortical inhibition of one image to avoid diplopia.
Amblyopia is reduced best-corrected acuity from abnormal visual experience in the critical period, without visible structural cause.
Heterophoria is latent and controlled by fusion; strabismus is manifest, and may be comitant or incomitant.
Cover tests, prism tests, suppression and stereoacuity tests guide management; correct refractive error first and follow current guidelines for amblyopia and strabismus.

en.title: Contact lens practice
en.short: Covers materials, designs, fitting, care, hygiene, patient selection, complications and referral.

sections.heading: Materials and designs
sections.text: Contact lenses are medical devices worn on the front of the eye. Soft lenses are made of hydrogel, a water-containing polymer, or silicone hydrogel, which allows more oxygen to reach the cornea. Rigid gas permeable (RGP) lenses are small rigid lenses. Scleral lenses are large rigid lenses that rest on the sclera and vault the cornea. Designs include spherical, toric for astigmatism and multifocal for presbyopia; lenses may be daily disposable or reusable.

sections.heading: Fitting and selection
sections.text: Fitting matches lens geometry to the eye. For soft lenses, check diameter, base curve (back-surface curve), centration, movement, comfort, vision and over-refraction. For RGP lenses, assess the fluorescein pattern, the tear layer seen with dye. For scleral lenses, check sagittal depth and corneal clearance. Patient selection considers motivation, dexterity, ocular surface health, refractive error, occupation and ability to follow hygiene. Active infection, uncontrolled dry eye, severe allergy and poor compliance are cautions or contraindications. Local law sets who may fit lenses.

sections.heading: Care and hygiene
sections.text: Daily disposable lenses are discarded after one wear. Reusable soft lenses need cleaning and disinfection with an approved system, such as a multipurpose solution or hydrogen peroxide system. RGP lenses need a cleaner, rinse and storage solution. Never use tap water, homemade saline or saliva. Wash and dry hands before handling. Clean and air-dry the case, and replace lenses and cases as instructed. Do not swim or shower in lenses. Follow manufacturer instructions and current national guidance.

sections.heading: Complications and referral
sections.text: Complications include dryness, discomfort, hypoxia (low oxygen), corneal oedema, neovascularisation (new vessels), infiltrative keratitis, microbial keratitis (corneal infection), giant papillary conjunctivitis and tight lens syndrome. Overnight wear, poor hygiene, smoking and water exposure raise risk. Case: Amina, 23, swims in a river with monthly soft lenses and later has a painful red eye and photophobia. Remove the lens and refer same day for slit-lamp assessment; do not use leftover drops. Urgent referral is needed for pain, photophobia, reduced vision, corneal opacity, infiltrate or no improvement after lens removal. Record findings and follow local pathways.

keyPoints: Contact lenses are medical devices; soft hydrogel and silicone hydrogel lenses differ in oxygen transmission, while RGP and scleral lenses are rigid designs.
Fitting checks lens geometry, movement, centration, vision and, for RGP lenses, the fluorescein pattern.
Patient selection depends on ocular surface health, motivation, dexterity and ability to follow hygiene.
Never use tap water, homemade saline or saliva with lenses or cases.
Overnight wear, poor hygiene, smoking and water exposure raise the risk of microbial keratitis.
Pain, photophobia, reduced vision or a corneal infiltrate after lens wear needs same-day referral.

en.title: Ocular pharmacology
en.short: Routes, drug classes, diagnostic agents, glaucoma drugs and adverse effects in eye care.

sections.heading: Routes of delivery
sections.text: Eye medicines are given by several routes. Topical drops and ointments are commonest. Drops act quickly but tears wash them away; ointments stay longer and may blur vision. Punctal occlusion, pressing the inner corner after a drop, reduces drainage into the nose and systemic absorption. Periocular injection places drug near the eye, such as subconjunctival or sub-Tenon. Intravitreal injection puts drug into the vitreous for retinal disease. Systemic drugs reach the eye through blood, but the blood-retinal and blood-aqueous barriers limit entry.

sections.heading: Drug classes
sections.text: Anti-infective drugs treat bacterial, viral and fungal eye infection. Choice depends on the likely organism and local resistance. Anti-inflammatory drugs include corticosteroids, which are powerful but can raise intraocular pressure, cause cataract and mask infection, and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Glaucoma drugs lower intraocular pressure, the pressure inside the eye, by reducing aqueous production or increasing outflow. Groups are prostaglandin analogues, beta blockers, alpha agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and cholinergic agonists. Hyperosmotics are used in severe cases. All groups can cause adverse effects; beta blockers can cause bradycardia and bronchospasm.

sections.heading: Diagnostic agents
sections.text: Diagnostic agents help examination rather than treat disease. Mydriatics widen the pupil for fundoscopy; cycloplegics also relax accommodation, useful when refracting children. Both can precipitate angle closure, so check depth and history. Topical anaesthetics numb the surface for tonometry or foreign body removal; they are not for repeated home use. Fluorescein stains damaged cornea and tears and is used with a blue light. Other dyes are used in specialist clinics.

sections.heading: Safety and formulary
sections.text: Topical drugs often cause stinging, blurred vision and allergy. Preservatives such as benzalkonium chloride can irritate the ocular surface. Systemic absorption can cause serious effects, so use punctal occlusion and review other medicines. A case: a patient with asthma given a topical beta blocker develops wheeze; the drug is stopped and the prescriber is told. Doses and cautions differ by country and change. Always check the current national formulary and local prescribing rules; this summary gives no doses.

keyPoints: Topical drops and ointments are the main ocular routes; punctal occlusion reduces systemic absorption.
Periocular and intravitreal injections place drug near or inside the eye; systemic drugs must cross blood-ocular barriers.
Anti-infectives are chosen from the likely organism and local resistance; corticosteroids can raise intraocular pressure, cause cataract and mask infection.
Glaucoma drugs lower intraocular pressure by reducing aqueous production or increasing outflow.
Mydriatics and cycloplegics aid examination but can precipitate angle closure in susceptible eyes.
Check the current national formulary for doses, indications and cautions; this summary gives no doses.

en.title: Anterior segment and adnexal disease
en.short: Lid, lacrimal, conjunctival, corneal, scleral and anterior uveal disease: signs, differentials and referral.

sections.heading: Lids and lacrimal system
sections.text: The lids and lacrimal system protect the eye. Blepharitis is lid margin inflammation with crusting. A hordeolum is an acute infected lid gland; a chalazion is a blocked, painless gland. Ectropion turns the lid out, entropion turns it in, and trichiasis is misdirected lashes rubbing the cornea. Epiphora is overflow of tears. Dacryocystitis is lacrimal sac infection, with painful swelling and discharge. Refer non-healing lid lesions, lash loss, entropion or trichiasis that threatens the cornea, and dacryocystitis.

sections.heading: Conjunctiva and cornea
sections.text: Conjunctivitis is conjunctival inflammation, with redness, discharge and discomfort; vision is usually normal. Keratitis is corneal inflammation. It causes pain, photophobia, tearing and reduced vision, with corneal opacity or fluorescein staining. A corneal ulcer is an epithelial defect with stromal inflammation or infection and is sight-threatening. Differentials for a red eye include bacterial, viral or allergic conjunctivitis, dry eye, foreign body, keratitis, anterior uveitis and acute glaucoma. Urgent referral is needed for severe pain, photophobia, reduced vision, contact lens wear with red eye, corneal infiltrate or ulcer, chemical injury (irrigate at once, then refer) or non-healing defect. Do not self-medicate with drops before assessment.

sections.heading: Sclera and anterior uvea
sections.text: Scleritis is deep scleral inflammation with severe pain, tenderness and violaceous (purple) eye; episcleritis is milder and superficial. Anterior uveitis is inflammation of iris and ciliary body. It causes pain, photophobia, redness around the cornea, small pupil and cells or protein haze in the anterior chamber. Differentials include keratitis, conjunctivitis, scleritis and acute glaucoma. Refer scleritis and anterior uveitis urgently. Hypopyon, a layer of white cells in the anterior chamber, is an emergency.

sections.heading: Case and referral
sections.text: Case: Amina, a 24-year-old contact lens wearer, has a painful right eye, photophobia and blurred vision. Fluorescein staining shows a corneal defect. This suggests microbial keratitis. Remove the lens, avoid patching and refer same day. Clinical guidelines change and differ by country; check national or World Health Organization guidance. This summary is education, not medical advice, and gives no treatment doses.

keyPoints: Blepharitis, hordeolum and chalazion are common lid margin or gland disorders; non-healing lid lesions need referral.
Epiphora and dacryocystitis point to lacrimal obstruction or infection; dacryocystitis needs prompt referral.
Conjunctivitis usually spares vision, while keratitis causes pain, photophobia and reduced vision.
A corneal ulcer, contact lens red eye, chemical injury or hypopyon is an emergency.
Scleritis causes severe pain; anterior uveitis causes photophobia and anterior chamber cells or protein haze.
Optometrists recognise, triage and refer; check current national or World Health Organization guidance rather than a fixed protocol.

en.title: Posterior segment disease
en.short: Vitreous, retinal, choroidal and optic nerve disease: detection, examples and referral.

sections.heading: Vitreous and the retina
sections.text:
The vitreous is the clear gel filling the eye behind the lens. With age it liquefies and shrinks, pulling on the retina. This causes floaters and flashes, and can tear the retina. A sudden shower of floaters, flashes, or a curtain across vision needs same-day referral.

The retina is neural tissue. Its outer layer, the retinal pigment epithelium, supports the photoreceptors. The choroid is the vascular layer beneath, supplying the outer retina.

sections.heading: Detachment and vascular occlusion
sections.text:
Retinal detachment means the neurosensory retina separates from the pigment epithelium. Rhegmatogenous detachment follows a retinal break. Tractional detachment follows pulling bands, as in diabetic retinopathy. Exudative detachment follows fluid leakage. All cause painless visual loss and are emergencies.

Retinal artery occlusion causes sudden painless loss with a pale retina. Retinal vein occlusion causes blurred vision with flame haemorrhages. Both link to hypertension, diabetes and cardiovascular risk, so patients need systemic assessment.

sections.heading: Macula, choroid and inheritance
sections.text:
Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) damages the macula, the centre of the retina. Dry AMD shows drusen, yellow deposits. Wet AMD shows choroidal neovascularisation, new vessels that leak. Inherited retinal diseases such as retinitis pigmentosa cause progressive night blindness and field loss, with pigmentary changes.

Choroidal disease includes naevi, melanoma and choroiditis. Colour vision, field testing and imaging help; genetic counselling may apply.

sections.heading: Optic nerve and referral
sections.text:
Optic neuropathy is damage to the optic nerve. Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy causes sudden painless loss with a swollen disc, often in older patients with vascular risk. Optic neuritis causes painful loss, worse on eye movement, and may signal multiple sclerosis. Compressive and toxic causes exist.

Refer urgently for sudden loss, a new field defect, a swollen disc or a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD, where the pupil dilates when light is swung to the affected eye). Optometrists detect and refer; treatment follows current national protocols and WHO-aligned guidance.

keyPoints: Sudden floaters, flashes or a visual curtain suggest retinal tear or detachment: refer the same day.
Rhegmatogenous detachment follows a break; tractional follows pulling bands; exudative follows leakage.
Dry AMD shows drusen; wet AMD shows choroidal neovascularisation.
Retinal vascular occlusion signals systemic vascular risk and needs medical assessment.
Optic neuritis is painful on eye movement; ischaemic optic neuropathy is usually painless.
A relative afferent pupillary defect points to optic nerve or extensive retinal disease.

en.title: Glaucoma
en.short: This summary covers glaucoma types, IOP, angle and disc assessment, field loss, monitoring, treatment and referral.

sections.heading: Types and pressure
sections.text:
Glaucoma is a group of optic neuropathies with progressive retinal ganglion cell and nerve fibre loss, usually linked to raised intraocular pressure (IOP). Main types are primary open-angle glaucoma, primary angle-closure glaucoma, secondary glaucomas (such as neovascular, pseudoexfoliative, uveitic or steroid-induced) and developmental or childhood glaucoma. Normal-tension glaucoma is open-angle glaucoma with IOP in the usual range.

IOP is the fluid pressure inside the eye, often quoted as 10 to 21 mmHg in adults. It is the main modifiable risk factor, but it is not the diagnosis: some people have glaucoma with IOP in that range, and some have ocular hypertension without optic nerve damage. Tonometry measures IOP; central corneal thickness affects the reading.

sections.heading: Angle, disc and field
sections.text:
Angle assessment asks whether the drainage angle is open or closed. Gonioscopy is the reference method; slit-lamp methods such as van Herick can suggest a narrow angle but do not replace gonioscopy. Acute angle closure causes pain, redness, blurred vision and a fixed pupil, and is an emergency.

Optic disc changes include increased cup-to-disc ratio, neuroretinal rim thinning, retinal nerve fibre layer loss and disc haemorrhage. Visual field testing may show an arcuate scotoma, a nasal step, a paracentral defect, or in advanced disease a small central island or tunnel vision.

Example: Mr Okafor, 60, has IOP 28 mmHg in the right eye, a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.8 and an arcuate field defect. Gonioscopy shows an open angle. This suggests primary open-angle glaucoma, so refer him for confirmation and treatment.

sections.heading: Monitoring and treatment
sections.text: Monitoring combines IOP, optic disc and retinal nerve fibre layer imaging, visual fields, adherence and risk factors; frequency follows severity and guidance. Treatment aims to lower IOP and slow progression. Options include topical medicines, laser (trabeculoplasty for open angle; peripheral iridotomy for angle closure), lens extraction for angle closure, and incisional surgery. Explain drop technique, side effects and cost, and check adherence. Refer suspected glaucoma, acute angle closure or rapid progression to ophthalmology. Use current national guidance.

keyPoints: Glaucoma is progressive optic neuropathy; IOP is the main modifiable risk factor but not the diagnosis.
Gonioscopy is the reference method for angle assessment.
Disc cupping, rim thinning and field defects such as arcuate scotoma support the diagnosis.
Treatment aims to lower IOP and slow progression using medicines, laser or surgery.
Check adherence and refer suspected glaucoma or acute angle closure promptly.
Follow current national guidance and local protocols.

en.title: Systemic disease and the eye
en.short: Covers ocular signs of diabetes, hypertension, HIV, TB, sickle cell, thyroid disease and medicines, plus referral.

sections.heading: Vascular and metabolic
sections.text:
Diabetes damages small retinal vessels. Non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy shows microaneurysms, dot and blot haemorrhages, hard exudates and cotton wool spots. Proliferative disease grows new vessels, which can bleed or detach the retina.

Hypertension narrows arterioles and may cause flame haemorrhages, cotton wool spots and, in malignant hypertension, papilloedema (swelling of the optic disc). A 54-year-old man with diabetes and blurred vision has dot haemorrhages and hard exudates; the optometrist records the findings and refers for ophthalmology review and diabetes care.

sections.heading: Infection and blood
sections.text:
HIV may cause HIV retinopathy with cotton wool spots, or opportunistic infection such as cytomegalovirus retinitis when immunity is low.

Tuberculosis can produce choroidal tubercles, uveitis or optic nerve involvement, but ocular TB is uncommon and needs specialist assessment. Sickle cell disease causes comma-shaped conjunctival vessels and retinal changes: salmon-patch haemorrhages, sea-fan neovascularisation and vitreous bleeding. These signs can appear before sight loss, so screening matters.

sections.heading: Thyroid and medicines
sections.text:
Thyroid eye disease, often linked to Graves disease, causes lid retraction, proptosis (bulging), diplopia and, rarely, optic neuropathy.

Medicines can affect the eye: corticosteroids raise cataract and glaucoma risk; hydroxychloroquine can cause maculopathy; ethambutol can cause optic neuropathy; and some drugs precipitate acute angle closure. Ask about all medicines, including traditional and over-the-counter products.

sections.heading: Referral
sections.text:
Refer urgently for sudden vision loss, ocular pain, papilloedema, new vessels, optic neuropathy or suspected systemic infection.

Otherwise refer non-urgently for unexplained ocular signs. Optometrists do not treat systemic disease; they document signs and send the patient to the appropriate physician or ophthalmologist. Screening intervals and treatment guidelines differ by country and change, so follow current national guidance or World Health Organization advice.

keyPoints: Diabetic retinopathy shows microaneurysms, haemorrhages, exudates and cotton wool spots; new vessels signal proliferative disease.
Hypertensive retinopathy includes arteriolar narrowing, flame haemorrhages and papilloedema in malignant hypertension.
HIV and tuberculosis can cause retinitis, choroidal tubercles or uveitis, especially when immunity is low.
Sickle cell disease causes comma-shaped conjunctival vessels and proliferative retinal changes such as sea-fan vessels.
Thyroid eye disease causes lid retraction, proptosis and diplopia; medicines such as corticosteroids and hydroxychloroquine can harm the eye.
Refer urgently for sudden vision loss, pain, papilloedema, new vessels or optic neuropathy, and follow current national or WHO guidance.

en.title: Paediatric optometry
en.short: Visual development, paediatric refraction, amblyopia, strabismus and school screening, paediatric eye disease, referral.

sections.heading: Visual development
sections.text:
Vision is immature at birth. Visual acuity, contrast sensitivity and stereopsis improve as the visual pathways and eye alignment develop. Stereopsis means depth perception from two eyes.

Most children reach adult acuity by school age, but the exact timing varies. The critical period is an early window when abnormal visual input can permanently affect vision. A child with cloudy media, misaligned eyes or very blurred focus needs early assessment.

sections.heading: Refraction and amblyopia
sections.text:
Paediatric refraction measures refractive error in children, who may not describe blur. Cycloplegic refraction uses eye drops to relax accommodation (the eye’s focusing power); it is often needed because children accommodate strongly.

Amblyopia is reduced vision in one or both eyes caused by abnormal visual experience, not by visible structural disease. Risks include strabismus (misalignment), anisometropia (unequal refractive error), high bilateral refractive error, ptosis (drooping eyelid) and media opacity (cloudiness inside the eye). Treatment aims to give a clear image and encourage use of the weaker eye; protocols vary, so follow current national guidance.

sections.heading: Screening and signs
sections.text:
Strabismus screening uses history, red reflex, cover test and acuity. School vision screening checks acuity and sometimes refraction; it cannot replace a full eye examination.

Paediatric eye disease includes congenital cataract, congenital glaucoma, ptosis and retinopathy of prematurity, a retinal disorder of preterm babies. Urgent referral is needed for absent red reflex, white pupil (leukocoria), infantile glaucoma signs such as watering, photophobia (light sensitivity) and a large cornea, or a new squint. Case: a 4-year-old with a constant inward turn and 6/18 in the turned eye is referred; unequal acuity plus strabismus raises amblyopia risk. Guidelines differ by country; check current national or WHO guidance.

sections.heading: Referral
sections.text:
Referral should state age, history, acuity, refraction and red reflex findings. Early referral matters because amblyopia treatment is more effective in young children.

Do not delay urgent cases for a routine appointment. Local referral pathways and screening intervals differ, so use current national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Vision and stereopsis mature in early childhood, and the critical period is when abnormal input can cause lasting loss.
Cycloplegic refraction is often needed in children because accommodation can hide refractive error.
Amblyopia is reduced vision from abnormal visual experience, not structural eye disease.
Risk factors include strabismus, anisometropia, high refractive error, ptosis and media opacity.
Red reflex, cover test and acuity are core screening checks; school screening does not replace full eye examination.
Urgent referral is needed for absent red reflex, leukocoria, infantile glaucoma signs or a new squint; follow current national or WHO guidance.

en.title: Low vision and rehabilitation
en.short: Functional vision assessment, magnification, optical and non-optical aids, lighting and team rehabilitation.

sections.heading: Functional assessment
sections.text: Low vision is reduced vision or a restricted visual field that ordinary spectacles, contact lenses, surgery or treatment cannot correct and that limits everyday activities. It is not the same as blindness. A functional vision assessment records the case history and the person’s goals, then measures distance and near visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, visual fields, glare sensitivity and reading performance. Testing only acuity misses problems such as poor contrast or a field loss. The assessment links findings to tasks like reading, cooking, walking and recognising faces.

sections.heading: Magnification and aids
sections.text:
Magnification makes the retinal image larger. It can be relative distance, by moving closer; relative size, by using larger print; angular, by using a telescope; or electronic, by using a video magnifier. A simple estimate is: magnification needed = current acuity denominator ÷ target acuity denominator, when the Snellen numerator is the same. For example, a person seeing 6/60 who wants to read 6/12 needs 60 ÷ 12 = 5× magnification. Check the arithmetic and the working distance.

Optical aids include hand and stand magnifiers, telescopes and prisms. Non-optical aids include large print, high contrast, typoscopes (slotted cards that isolate lines), reading stands, audio books and screen readers. Use task lighting from the side, control glare and improve contrast. The choice depends on the task, the field of view and the person’s needs.

sections.heading: Training and team
sections.text: Training teaches skills, not just devices. Eccentric viewing uses a healthy part of the retina when the macula is damaged. Scanning and steady eye strategies help with reading and finding objects. Orientation and mobility training teaches safe movement, often with a cane. Rehabilitation is multidisciplinary: the optometrist, ophthalmologist, low vision therapist, occupational therapist, orientation and mobility instructor, teacher and social worker each contribute. Services and funding vary by country, so check current national guidance and local referral pathways.

keyPoints: Low vision is vision loss or a restricted visual field that ordinary glasses, contact lenses, surgery or treatment cannot correct and that limits daily activities.
Functional assessment covers acuity, contrast sensitivity, fields, glare and the person’s goals.
Magnification needed = current acuity denominator ÷ target acuity denominator when Snellen numerators match.
A person seeing 6/60 who needs 6/12 needs 5× magnification.
Optical aids include magnifiers and telescopes; non-optical aids include lighting, contrast and large print.
Training includes eccentric viewing, scanning and orientation and mobility, within a multidisciplinary team.

en.title: Ocular emergencies and trauma: triage and first aid
en.short: Triage red eye, chemical and foreign-body injury, trauma, angle closure and sudden vision loss.

sections.heading: Red eye triage
sections.text: Triage means sorting by urgency, not diagnosing. Most red eyes are due to conjunctivitis or dry eye, but danger signs change the plan: severe pain, photophobia (light sensitivity), reduced vision, ciliary flush (redness around the cornea), corneal opacity, a fixed or mid-dilated pupil, trauma, or contact lens wear. These need same-day eye review. A farmer hit by a branch with a fixed pupil and blurred vision is an emergency, not a simple red eye.

sections.heading: Chemical and foreign body
sections.text: Chemical injury is a true emergency. Start copious irrigation with clean water or saline at once, before transfer, remove contact lenses if present, and evert the lids to remove particles. Do not wait for pH measurement or use antidotes. A superficial foreign body may be removed if it is visible and not embedded; never rub the eye or attempt removal of an embedded or central object. Refer all chemical injuries and any foreign body with visual change or pain.

sections.heading: Blunt and open-globe trauma
sections.text: Blunt trauma can cause hyphema (blood in the anterior chamber), blowout fracture, or retinal detachment. Protect the eye, avoid pressure, and refer urgently. In an open-globe (penetrating or perforating) injury, do not remove a stuck object. Place a rigid shield over the eye without pressing, and send the patient for urgent surgical assessment. Do not give eye drops or pressure patches unless local protocol directs.

sections.heading: Acute angle closure and sudden vision loss
sections.text: Acute angle closure presents with severe eye or head pain, nausea, halos, a hazy cornea, and a mid-dilated pupil. It needs immediate referral. Sudden vision loss may be painless, as in retinal artery occlusion or detachment, or painful, as in angle closure or keratitis. Check visual acuity in each eye and pupillary reactions, then refer the same day. First aid is limited to protection and transport. National and WHO guidance change, so check current local protocols.

keyPoints: Triage the red eye by danger signs: severe pain, photophobia, reduced vision, ciliary flush, corneal opacity, fixed pupil, trauma or contact lens wear.
Chemical injury needs immediate copious irrigation and urgent referral; do not delay for pH or antidotes.
Do not remove an embedded or penetrating object; shield the eye without pressure.
Blunt trauma can cause hyphema, blowout fracture or retinal detachment and needs urgent review.
Acute angle closure and sudden vision loss need same-day referral.
Check visual acuity and pupils in every eye emergency, and follow current national or WHO guidance.

en.title: Public health optometry
en.short: Blindness burden, screening, WHO and national guidance, health promotion, and equitable eye care access.

sections.heading: Burden and causes
sections.text: Public health optometry studies eye disease in populations. The burden of blindness and vision impairment is the number affected plus the disability, economic and social costs. Causes vary by region and age. Globally, uncorrected refractive error and cataract are major causes; glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration, trachoma and onchocerciasis matter. In Africa, trachoma and onchocerciasis are important preventable causes. Figures change; use current WHO and national data.

sections.heading: Screening
sections.text: Screening tests apparently healthy people to find those needing further assessment. It is not diagnosis. A programme needs an important condition, an acceptable and accurate test, effective treatment, clear referral and monitoring for harm. Sensitivity is the proportion with the condition who test positive; specificity is the proportion without it who test negative. Example: of 1,000 people, 100 have the condition. The test finds 80, so sensitivity is 80/100 = 80%. It wrongly flags 90 of the 900 without it, so specificity is 810/900 = 90%.

sections.heading: Guidance and promotion
sections.text: WHO’s World report on vision (2019) and its integrated people-centred eye care approach call for eye care within universal health coverage. National ministries of health set eye health policy, screening priorities, workforce and medicines lists. These differ by country and change, so check current national and WHO guidance. Health promotion enables people to protect their eyes and seek care early. It includes tobacco control, diabetes and hypertension control, injury prevention, immunisation and vitamin A programmes. It works through policy, communities and services, not advice alone.

sections.heading: Access and equity
sections.text: Access means care is available, affordable, acceptable and reachable. Barriers include cost, distance, transport, workforce shortages, low awareness and stigma. Equity means fair access for rural communities, women, children, older people, people with disabilities and poor households. A free but distant clinic may still exclude people. Outreach, school screening, task-sharing with trained community workers and affordable spectacles can improve access. Public health optometry measures who is missed and why, then tests solutions.

keyPoints: The burden of blindness is the number affected plus disability, economic and social costs.
Screening is for apparently healthy people and needs clear referral, not diagnosis.
Sensitivity is true positives divided by all people with the condition; specificity is true negatives divided by all people without it.
WHO’s World report on vision (2019) supports integrated people-centred eye care within universal health coverage.
National eye health policy and screening priorities differ by country and change, so check current guidance.
Access barriers include cost, distance and workforce shortages; equity targets groups most often missed.

en.title: Optometry ethics, law and professionalism
en.short: Consent, confidentiality, records, scope of practice, regulation, referral and professional boundaries.

sections.heading: Consent and capacity
sections.text: Consent is permission given freely by an informed patient. It needs three things: information, capacity and no pressure. Explain the test, its risks, alternatives and what happens if nothing is done. Capacity is the ability to understand, retain, weigh and communicate a decision; adults are presumed to have it. Children and adults who lack capacity need a substitute decision maker under national law, which varies; England and Wales, for example, use the Mental Capacity Act 2005. Record the discussion.

sections.heading: Confidentiality and records
sections.text: Confidentiality means keeping patient information private. Share it only with those who need it, with consent, or where the law requires disclosure, such as a court order or a notifiable disease. Records are legal documents: write them at the time, date and sign them, and keep them accurate and secure, because patients may read them. Data protection law is national, for example the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 or the UK GDPR.

sections.heading: Scope and regulation
sections.text: Scope of practice is the set of acts a practitioner is trained and licensed to perform. Optometry is regulated country by country. In Nigeria the regulator is the Optometrists and Dispensing Opticians Registration Board of Nigeria; in the UK it is the General Optical Council. These bodies set registration, continuing education and fitness to practise rules. Working outside your scope is a disciplinary matter, even with a good result. Check your own board’s current guidelines.

sections.heading: Referral and boundaries
sections.text:
Referral passes care to someone with the needed skill, with the patient’s knowledge. Write the reason, your findings, what you have done and what you need. Urgent problems go the same day, not to a routine review.

Case: a 60-year-old woman reports sudden painless loss of vision in one eye. That pattern suggests a vascular or retinal cause, so refer urgently the same day.

Boundaries: avoid treating close family where judgement may be clouded, disclose any financial interest in a sale, and never exploit the power imbalance between clinician and patient.

keyPoints: Valid consent needs information, capacity and freedom from pressure, and it should be recorded.
Capacity is decision-specific; adults are presumed to have it, and national law governs children and adults who lack it.
Keep patient information confidential except with consent or where the law requires disclosure.
Clinical records are legal documents: contemporaneous, dated, signed and secure.
Scope of practice and registration are set by a national regulator, so check your own board’s rules.
Refer clearly and urgently when needed, and declare any financial interest in what you recommend.

en.title: Clinical optometry and case management
en.short: History, examination sequence, reasoning, communication, records, referral and follow-up in optometry.

sections.heading: History and examination sequence
sections.text: History taking is a structured conversation that records the patient’s main complaint, its onset and course, associated symptoms, past eye and general health, medicines, allergies, family history, work and social setting. Ask open questions first, then clarify. A red flag is a symptom or sign that suggests serious or urgent disease, such as sudden vision loss or severe pain. The examination sequence usually runs from general observation and visual acuity through pupils, eye movements, anterior segment, intraocular pressure and fundus, adjusted to the complaint. Record each result as found, not as expected.

sections.heading: Clinical reasoning and differential diagnosis
sections.text: Clinical reasoning means using history and findings to build a problem list, form hypotheses and test them. A differential diagnosis is a ranked list of possible explanations, not one guess. For each problem, ask what fits, what does not, and which serious condition must be excluded. In the case, Amina, a 52-year-old teacher, reports gradual blur and late-day headaches, with no sudden loss, severe pain or trauma. Distance acuity is reduced and the rest of the examination is unremarkable. The problem list is reduced distance acuity and headache. The differential includes refractive, binocular and ocular surface causes, covered elsewhere. With no red flag, routine review is arranged; she is told to return sooner if pain or sudden change occurs.

sections.heading: Communication, records, referral
sections.text: Communication uses plain language, open questions and teach-back, where the patient repeats the plan in their own words. Obtain consent before examination and keep information confidential. Records should be dated, signed and legible, with symptoms, findings, problem list, plan and advice. Avoid unclear abbreviations. Referral is the transfer of care for an opinion or procedure. State the reason, urgency, relevant history and findings, and what the patient has been told. Follow-up closes the loop: check that the referral happened, review the patient, and record the outcome. Follow current local and national referral criteria, and World Health Organization guidance where relevant. This summary is education, not medical advice.

keyPoints: Take a structured history before examining, and ask open questions first.
A red flag is a symptom or sign that suggests serious or urgent disease.
Clinical reasoning builds a problem list and tests hypotheses; a differential diagnosis is a ranked list of possible explanations.
Record dated, signed, legible findings and the plan, and avoid unclear abbreviations.
A referral should state the reason, urgency, relevant findings and what the patient has been told.
Follow-up closes the loop by checking that the referral happened and recording the outcome.

en.title: Advanced ocular imaging and diagnostics
en.short: Principles and limits of OCT, topography, biometry, ultrasound, visual fields and fundus imaging.

sections.heading: OCT and topography
sections.text: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) uses low-coherence light interference to build cross-sectional images.
