Retinal OCT shows layers, fluid and thickness maps; anterior-segment OCT shows the cornea and angle. Interpret by checking scan quality, segmentation and comparison with a normative database. Do not diagnose from one abnormal map. Corneal topography maps anterior curvature and elevation. It detects astigmatism and keratoconus patterns. Tear film, contact lenses and poor fixation cause artefacts. For example, if K1 is 42.00 D and K2 is 44.00 D, mean K = (42.00 + 44.00) ÷ 2 = 43.00 D, and astigmatism = 44.00 − 42.00 = 2.00 D.

sections.heading: Biometry and ultrasound
sections.text: Biometry measures axial length, keratometry and anterior chamber depth for intraocular lens power calculation. Optical biometry uses partial coherence interferometry and is usually non-contact. Ultrasound A-scan measures axial length when media are opaque; B-scan shows anatomy behind cataract or haemorrhage. Ultrasound biomicroscopy uses high frequency sound for the anterior segment. Limitations include dense cataract, poor fixation, contact technique and operator skill. Values must be checked against the other eye and previous records.

sections.heading: Fields and fundus
sections.text: Visual field perimetry maps sensitivity across the field. Threshold testing estimates the weakest light seen at points. Reliability indices, learning effects and variability limit interpretation, especially in glaucoma. Fundus imaging includes colour photography, autofluorescence and angiography. It documents optic disc, macula and vessels. Media opacity, small pupils and poor focus reduce quality. Imaging supports but does not replace slit-lamp and fundus examination.

sections.heading: Limits and safety
sections.text: All devices have resolution, penetration and artefact limits. Normative databases may not match every population. Guidelines differ by country, so follow current national or World Health Organization guidance and local protocols. This is education, not medical advice.

keyPoints: OCT uses low-coherence light to show cross-sectional structure and thickness; always check scan quality and segmentation.
Corneal topography maps curvature and elevation and is sensitive to tear film, contact lens and fixation artefacts.
Biometry measures axial length, keratometry and anterior chamber depth for intraocular lens power; optical and ultrasound methods have different limits.
Mean keratometry = (flat K + steep K) ÷ 2; astigmatism = steep K − flat K.
Visual field results depend on reliability indices, learning and variability, so they are interpreted with the clinical picture.
Fundus imaging documents the disc, macula and vessels but does not replace examination, and guidelines vary by country.

en.title: Advanced contact lens practice and the ocular surface
en.short: Specialist lens designs, keratoconus, scleral and post-surgical fitting, ocular surface disease and complications.

sections.heading: Specialist designs
sections.text:
Specialist lenses are used when soft lenses cannot correct vision or protect the surface. Rigid gas permeable (RGP) lenses are firm lenses that replace the cornea’s irregular front surface with a regular optical surface.

Toric lenses correct astigmatism, multifocal lenses correct presbyopia, and orthokeratology lenses temporarily reshape the cornea during overnight wear. Hybrid lenses combine a rigid centre with a soft skirt. Fitting depends on corneal shape, tear film, lid position and the person’s needs.

sections.heading: Keratoconus and scleral lenses
sections.text:
Keratoconus is progressive corneal thinning and bulging that causes irregular astigmatism. Spectacles often cannot give sharp vision. RGP lenses can improve vision by creating a regular surface.

A scleral lens is a large rigid lens that rests on the sclera and vaults the cornea, holding a fluid reservoir. It protects the surface and suits severe keratoconus or ocular surface disease. For example, Amina, a student with keratoconus, gains sharper vision and comfort from a scleral lens after RGP lenses irritated her cone. Corneal cross-linking is a medical treatment to slow progression; fitting follows ophthalmology advice.

sections.heading: Surgery and surface disease
sections.text:
After corneal transplant or refractive surgery, the cornea may be irregular, sensitive or have reduced sensation. Wait until the eye is stable and the surgeon agrees. Scleral or rigid lenses may help, but sutures, grafts and flap edges need care.

Ocular surface disease includes dry eye, meibomian gland dysfunction and limbal stem cell deficiency. A healthy tear film is essential for lens tolerance, so treat surface disease first where possible.

sections.heading: Complications and evidence
sections.text:
Complications include hypoxia, abrasion, solution toxicity, giant papillary conjunctivitis, corneal neovascularisation and microbial keratitis. Microbial keratitis is a sight-threatening infection and needs urgent referral.

Evidence comes from trials, cohort studies, registries and guidelines. Not every design has strong trial evidence. Guidelines differ by country and change, so check current national optometry or ophthalmology guidance and WHO advice rather than quoting a fixed protocol.

keyPoints: Specialist lenses include RGP, toric, multifocal, orthokeratology, hybrid and scleral designs.
Keratoconus causes irregular astigmatism; RGP or scleral lenses can restore a regular optical surface.
A scleral lens rests on the sclera and vaults the cornea, holding a fluid reservoir.
Post-surgical fitting waits for stability and surgical agreement; sutures and grafts need care.
Ocular surface disease should be treated for lens tolerance; microbial keratitis is an urgent referral.
Evidence varies by design; follow current national and WHO guidance, not a fixed protocol.

en.title: Advanced binocular vision and vision therapy
en.short: Complex strabismus, amblyopia therapy, convergence insufficiency, outcome measures and evidence.

sections.heading: Complex strabismus
sections.text: Strabismus is misalignment of the eyes. Complex cases are incomitant (deviation changes with gaze), restrictive or paretic, or follow surgery or thyroid eye disease. Assessment uses history, acuity, cover tests with prisms, eye movements and sensory tests. Suppression is the brain ignoring one image; anomalous retinal correspondence is abnormal pairing of retinal points. These adaptations can limit treatment. Management may use refractive correction, prisms, surgery and vision therapy as an adjunct. Protocols differ by country; follow current national guidance.

sections.heading: Amblyopia therapy
sections.text: Amblyopia is reduced best-corrected acuity caused by abnormal visual experience, not structural disease. Causes include anisometropia (unequal refractive error), strabismus and deprivation. Treat the cause first: correct refractive error and remove obstruction such as cataract. Then encourage use of the amblyopic eye with occlusion or atropine penalisation; atropine is a medicine, so dose and monitoring follow local protocol. Adherence and review matter; excessive occlusion can cause reverse amblyopia in the other eye. Binocular and digital treatments are being studied; evidence is still developing.

sections.heading: Convergence insufficiency
sections.text: Convergence insufficiency is a near-vision disorder with exophoria greater at near than distance, reduced positive fusional vergence and a receded near point of convergence (NPC). Symptoms include eyestrain, headaches and blur after reading. Illustrative case: a student has 8 prism dioptres exophoria at near, 2 at distance, NPC break at 14 cm and near positive fusional vergence of 8 prism dioptres. Therapy uses vergence and accommodative exercises, often office-based with home reinforcement. Randomised trials such as the Convergence Insufficiency Treatment Trial found office-based therapy better than some home pencil push-up regimens for several outcomes.

sections.heading: Outcomes and evidence
sections.text: Outcome measures should cover symptoms, binocular status (NPC, fusional vergence, stereoacuity), acuity, adherence, quality of life and adverse effects. Evidence comes from randomised trials and systematic reviews, but studies are small, unmasked and use different protocols. Controversies include office-based versus home therapy, duration, surgery for convergence insufficiency, and how much vision therapy helps beyond placebo. Check current national optometry or ophthalmology guidance; WHO guidance addresses health systems, not protocols.

keyPoints: Complex strabismus is often incomitant or restrictive; assess eye movements and sensory adaptation.
Suppression and anomalous retinal correspondence can limit binocular recovery.
Treat amblyopia’s cause first, then use occlusion or atropine penalisation under local protocol.
Convergence insufficiency combines near exophoria, reduced positive fusional vergence and receded NPC.
Outcome measures include symptoms, NPC, fusional vergence, stereoacuity, acuity and adherence.
Evidence supports office-based vergence therapy for many patients, but protocols and controversies remain; check current national guidance.

en.title: Research methods and dissertation in optometry
en.short: Study design, sampling, measurement, ethics, statistics, critical appraisal and dissertation writing in optometry.

sections.heading: Design and sampling
sections.text: Study design is the plan for answering the question. Observational designs include cross-sectional surveys, cohort studies and case-control studies. Experimental designs, such as randomised controlled trials, test an intervention by comparing groups. Sampling selects participants from a sampling frame, the list of the population. Probability methods include simple random, stratified and cluster sampling; non-probability methods include convenience and purposive sampling. Probability sampling supports generalisation. Sample size depends on effect size, variability, power and dropout.

sections.heading: Measurement and ethics
sections.text: Measurement must be valid, meaning it measures the intended construct, and reliable, meaning repeated measurements agree. Calibrate instruments, standardise procedures and train observers. Blinding reduces bias. Research ethics requires approval from a research ethics committee, informed consent, confidentiality and fair selection. Vulnerable groups need extra protection. Follow current national regulations and World Health Organization guidance; do not rely on a fixed protocol. Record adverse events and conflicts of interest.

sections.heading: Statistics and appraisal
sections.text:
Statistics describe data and test hypotheses. Descriptive statistics summarise with means, medians and standard deviations. Inferential statistics use p-values and 95% confidence intervals; a confidence interval shows the range of plausible values. Critical appraisal asks whether the question, design, sampling, measurement and analysis support the conclusions. Sensitivity is the proportion with the condition who test positive; specificity is the proportion without it who test negative.

Example: in 200 patients, 40 have a condition. The test is positive in 20 of them. Of 160 without the condition, 16 test positive. Sensitivity is 20 ÷ 40 = 50%. Specificity is (160 − 16) ÷ 160 = 144 ÷ 160 = 90%.

sections.heading: Dissertation planning
sections.text: Plan the dissertation around a focused question and a short literature review. Write a protocol with aims, methods, ethics, data analysis and timeline. Keep a research diary and back up data. The report usually follows Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion. State limitations honestly. Use a consistent referencing style. Check your institution’s rules and word limit. Prepare for a viva by explaining your choices and defending your conclusions.

keyPoints: A focused research question guides the design, sampling, measurement and analysis.
Probability sampling supports generalisation; convenience sampling risks bias.
Valid and reliable measurement needs calibration, standardisation and blinding.
Ethics approval, informed consent and confidentiality are required; follow current national and WHO guidance.
Sensitivity = true positives ÷ all with the condition; specificity = true negatives ÷ all without it.
Critical appraisal and honest limitations strengthen a dissertation and its viva.
